Physics · Energy · ABOUT 20 MINUTES

A torch lights the room. What changes elsewhere?

Energy connects food, fuels, movement, heating and electricity. Tracking where it is stored and how it is transferred helps us explain what a device does, what it needs and why it eventually stops.

START WITH A QUESTION

Imagine a battery torch left shining until it goes dark. Has the energy disappeared, or would you expect changes in the battery, torch and room? Predict which things might warm up.

Have a guess together before revealing the idea.

The idea underneath +

The battery’s chemical energy store decreases as energy is transferred electrically through the circuit. Light carries energy away; absorbed light increases thermal stores in the surroundings. The torch also warms. Energy is conserved when the whole account includes the surroundings. Useful changes can involve kinetic stores of moving objects, gravitational stores of raised objects, elastic stores of stretched objects or thermal stores. Energy transfers can happen through heating, electrical currents, forces moving objects, and radiation such as light.

Why know this?

Energy accounts help compare appliances and understand why insulation matters. Power tells us how quickly energy is transferred: one watt means one joule per second. A powerful appliance used briefly can transfer less energy overall than a lower-power appliance left on for hours.

01

Lunch can lift a backpack

Your body transfers energy from chemical stores as you lift a bag. Its gravitational store increases, and your body and surroundings also warm.

02

Insulation buys time

Insulation slows energy transfer between warmer and cooler places. It does not supply an endless source of warmth.

03

Useful depends on the job

Warming is useful in a heater. Warming a torch casing is usually an unwanted transfer when the aim is illumination.

THINK / DRAW / TRY

Make it a conversation.

Draw a battery torch inside a larger box labelled room. Add arrows showing electrical transfer within the torch, light leaving it and heating of its surroundings. Label the starting chemical store and final thermal stores. Now imagine two devices: one transfers 10 joules each second for 20 seconds, the other 5 joules each second for 60 seconds. Predict which transfers more energy, then multiply to check.

One more twist

If energy is never destroyed, why do we need fresh batteries or more food? Could the energy spread around the room simply do the same job again?

Help me explain this +

The opening account should include the battery, torch and room. A tiny temperature rise can be real without being noticeable by touch. For the twist, energy spread among the surroundings is less available for the desired job; conservation does not promise endless reuse. Fresh batteries provide an accessible chemical store. The calculation gives 200 J and 300 J: duration matters as well as power. Listen for a distinction between how much energy and how quickly it moves. Stores and arrows are bookkeeping tools, not containers and pipes of an invisible substance. Light is a transfer pathway in this model, not a permanent store.

A common mix-up

Energy and power are not interchangeable. Joules measure an amount of energy; watts measure the rate of transfer.

Think like a scientist

How could you compare two torches fairly? Consider brightness, starting battery condition and operating time before deciding what “better” means.
